references.text: Jesus says that one must turn and become like a child to enter the kingdom of heaven. This is the parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus uses the same image of receiving God's kingdom as a child ([ref:Matt 18:3|Matthew 18:3]).
Mark's parallel to this verse, where Jesus says the same thing: Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it ([ref:Mark 10:15|Mark 10:15]).

Matthew's parallel account about Jesus and the children, where Jesus says "Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these" ([ref:Matt 19:14|Matthew 19:14]).
Mark's parallel where Jesus becomes angry with the disciples and says that the kingdom of God belongs to little children ([ref:Mark 10:14|Mark 10:14]).

The immediately preceding verse where Jesus calls the children to him and says that the kingdom of God belongs to such as these, which forms the context for the statement in verse 17 ([ref:Luk 18:16|Luke 18:16]).

Jesus points out that whoever makes themselves like a child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. The humility and trust that characterize a child are necessary to receive God's kingdom ([ref:Matt 18:4|Matthew 18:4]).
Paul urges the Corinthians not to be children in understanding, but in evil. This touches on the theme of childlike innocence and trust ([ref:1 Kor 14:20|1 Corinthians 14:20]).

Peter encourages believers to long like newborn babies for pure spiritual milk, so that by it they may grow up in their salvation. The image of a child receiving with trust and dependence connects to Jesus' words about receiving the kingdom of God like a child ([ref:1 Pet 2:2|1 Peter 2:2]).

Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one can see or enter the kingdom of God without being born again. The theme of new birth and becoming like a child to enter God's kingdom is closely related ([ref:Joh 3:3-5|John 3:3-5]).
